content: Valley Forge General Hospital was a former military hospital located in Phoenixville, Pennsylvania, near both Philadelphia and Valley Forge. It was the only United States Army General Hospital named after a specific place. The hospital was constructed in 1942 and officially opened on Washington's Birthday in 1943 to provide care for wounded soldiers during World War II. It eventually became the largest military hospital in the United States, accommodating over 3,000 patients and consisting of more than 100 separate buildings. The hospital's design featured primarily two-story buildings interconnected by corridors, with long ramps facilitating the movement of wheelchairs and gurneys. The exterior was constructed of red brick, resembling a New England college campus, while the interior was made entirely of wood, typical of military buildings from the World War II era. The layout was complex, often causing newly assigned personnel to become lost in the maze of corridors. Although the hospital was initially slated for closure in 1950, the onset of the Korean War delayed its shutdown. It ultimately ceased operations as a hospital in 1974 and was officially closed in 1975. The site is now occupied by Valley Forge Christian College. Valley Forge General Hospital was featured in the 1951 film Bright Victory, which highlighted the rehabilitation of blinded soldiers. Many of the techniques for rehabilitating individuals with blindness were first developed and implemented at this hospital, making it one of the foremost medical units in the world for such care. The acrylic eye, a prosthetic for individuals who had lost an eyeball, was invented by one of the hospital's dentists and remains in use today. The hospital's Department of Psychiatry and Neurology was a global leader in psychiatric treatments, pioneering the use of new medications and therapeutic techniques. The medical staff, including physicians, nurses, and neuropsychiatric technicians, successfully returned tens of thousands of treated personnel to active duty, achieving a return-to-duty rate significantly higher than that of most civilian hospitals. Gene Wilder, the renowned actor, served as a neuropsychiatric technician at Valley Forge General Hospital in the late 1950s. In the late 1960s, the hospital became the site of a Clinical Specialist training program for military personnel (MOS 91C). This advanced nine-month training program required candidates to have at least two years of prior experience as medics and a minimum of two years remaining on their enlistment after completing the program. The training was rigorous and comprehensive, building on all previous medical training and experience. Personnel stationed at Valley Forge General Hospital did not have access to on-site married housing and instead rented accommodations in nearby communities such as Phoenixville, Norristown, and Pottstown. Many of them became active members of local groups and organizations. All enlisted personnel assigned to the hospital were required to undergo basic fire training, which included learning to use fire hoses, nozzles, and other firefighting equipment, as well as driving fire trucks. This training was essential due to the hospital's wooden interior and interconnected buildings, which posed a significant fire risk. Many married enlisted personnel also joined local volunteer fire departments, where their training proved valuable. After the release of the film Bright Victory, all hospital personnel were required to watch the movie. In the late 1960s, the hospital underwent extensive upgrades costing millions of dollars. However, shortly thereafter, the new Surgeon General of the United States Army determined that the hospital was no longer needed, leading to its closure. This decision was a significant loss for both the military and the local community.
